title: FRM Liquidity, Lesson 1: Bank liquidity risk - LCR and NSFR
subtitle: The two Basel III ratios written after 2008 to answer: does the bank survive a month of panic, and is its funding structure sustainable over the long run
whyItMatters: Before 2008 a bank counted as safe if it had enough capital. But Lehman Brothers and Northern Rock failed because they ran out of liquidity, not because they were insolvent in the accounting sense. LCR and NSFR are the two Basel III ratios created specifically to measure liquidity risk, entirely separately from capital risk.
openingQuestion: What does the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) measure?
openingOptions: The ratio of shareholders' equity to total risk-weighted assets
Enough liquid assets to withstand 30 straight days of stress
The ratio of non-performing loans to the total loan book
How well diversified the bank's investment portfolio is
explanation: LCR = High-Quality Liquid Assets (HQLA) / expected net cash outflow over a 30-day stress period, with a minimum of 100%. It is the short-term survival test: if depositors withdraw en masse and the interbank market freezes for a month, does the bank hold enough assets convertible into cash quickly enough to meet the demand?

diagram.label: Run the 30-day stress scenario: deposit withdrawals, credit lines pulled
LCR = HQLA / net cash outflow, at 100% or above
NSFR then tests stable funding over one year, not just 30 days

realWorldExample.description: This British bank had a balance sheet that looked healthy on capital, but it leaned heavily on short-term wholesale funding to finance long-term mortgage lending. When credit markets froze in mid-2007, Northern Rock could not roll its short-term funding, which produced the first queue of depositors outside a British bank in more than a hundred years - even though the bank was never insolvent in the traditional accounting sense. It is the textbook case that pushed LCR and NSFR into existence.

quiz.question: What is the core difference between LCR and NSFR?
options: NSFR measures credit risk while LCR measures market risk exposure
LCR is for retail banks and NSFR is for investment banks instead
Both measure exactly the same thing, only presented differently
LCR tests 30-day survival; NSFR tests stable funding over a year
quiz.explanation: LCR is the short-horizon test: thirty days, under an acute crisis scenario. NSFR, the Net Stable Funding Ratio, is the structural test over a longer horizon - available stable funding against required stable funding - and it exists to stop banks repeating Northern Rock's mistake of feeding long-dated assets with short-dated money. Neither ratio measures credit or market risk, both apply across bank business models, and the horizons are what separate them rather than the presentation.

quiz.question: Why did Northern Rock fail even though it looked well capitalised by pre-2008 standards?
options: Because it funded long-dated lending with short-term wholesale money
Because management committed outright fraud in the financial statements
Because its deposit funding rates sat far above the prevailing market
Because non-performing loans made up too much of its book
quiz.explanation: This is funding maturity mismatch in its purest form: long-dated assets - mortgages running 20 to 30 years - financed with short-dated debt that has to be rolled continuously. When the refinancing market freezes, that structure collapses regardless of whether the capital adequacy ratio meets the standard, which is exactly the failure NSFR was later designed to prevent. The loan book performed adequately, the accounts were not falsified, and the cost of funding was ordinary; the tenor of the funding was the flaw.

quiz.question: In the LCR formula, what characteristic must High-Quality Liquid Assets (HQLA) have?
options: They must be the highest-yielding assets held in the bank's portfolio
They convert into cash quickly at minimal discount
Any asset that happens to sit on the balance sheet counts towards it
Only loans secured against real estate count towards the total
quiz.explanation: HQLA has to satisfy two conditions at once: it must be liquid enough to sell quickly, and its value must hold up even when markets are under stress - unlike equities or property, which can lose liquidity or fall sharply in price at precisely the moment they need to be sold, which is when everyone else is panicking too. High yield is a signal of the opposite property, and a general balance sheet total says nothing about how fast any of it can be turned into cash.

quiz.question: Why do supervisors need a dedicated liquidity metric rather than relying on the capital adequacy ratio?
options: Because the capital adequacy ratio already covers every aspect of liquidity risk, so a separate metric only adds reporting complexity for no gain
Because Basel rules before 2008 had never touched on the concept of bank capital at all in any of the published frameworks
Because a bank that is adequately capitalised on paper can still fail if it lacks the cash to meet short-term obligations during a run - two independent risks
Because liquidity risk only shows up at small banks and never affects large ones, so capital rules are enough for the majors
quiz.explanation: This is the central lesson of 2008: solvency - assets exceeding liabilities - and liquidity - having enough cash at the moment it is demanded - are different problems. An adequately capitalised institution can still fail if its assets cannot be turned into cash quickly enough to meet short-term obligations. Capital rules long predate 2008 and say nothing about timing, and the largest institutions have proved just as vulnerable, since wholesale funding disappears fastest exactly where it is largest.

quiz.question: Why can a well-capitalised bank still fail within a few days?
options: Because loan losses are recognised more slowly than the cash going out
Because the capital adequacy ratio is only recalculated at each quarter end
Because a supervisor can demand a capital increase as soon as bad news lands
Because capital cannot be turned into cash to pay the people withdrawing
quiz.explanation: Capital measures the ability to absorb losses; liquidity measures the ability to pay today. A bank can be well capitalised on paper while all of its assets sit in long-dated loans it cannot sell in time - which is exactly why Basel had to add two separate ratios for liquidity. The recognition lag and the reporting frequency are real accounting issues, but neither of them is what stops a queue of depositors from being paid on the afternoon it forms.

practicePrompt.question: A bank runs a capital adequacy ratio (CAR) of 15%, far above the minimum, but 70% of its funding comes from one-week interbank borrowing used to finance a five-year corporate loan book. What is the biggest risk here?
options: Nothing material, because the capital adequacy ratio is already high
Funding maturity mismatch, exactly the Northern Rock pattern
Interest rate risk alone, with no bearing on liquidity at all
The bank should simply raise more equity to solve the problem
practicePrompt.explanation: This is precisely Northern Rock's risk structure: a high capital ratio does nothing for a funding maturity mismatch. The right fix is to diversify funding towards longer tenors - which is what NSFR measures - rather than to add more shareholders' equity.

keyTakeaways: LCR = HQLA / net cash outflow under a 30-day stress scenario, minimum 100% - the short-term survival test
NSFR tests the stability of the funding structure over a one-year horizon, preventing a mismatch between short-dated funding and long-dated assets
Northern Rock (2007) failed while adequately capitalised, because it funded long-dated mortgage assets with short-term wholesale money - exactly what NSFR was designed to prevent
Solvency and liquidity are independent risks - having enough capital does not mean having enough cash at the moment it is needed

summary.keyIdea: Being well capitalised and being liquid are two independent things. Northern Rock failed while still adequately capitalised, because short-term wholesale funding vanished faster than long-dated assets could be sold.
summary.formula: LCR = HQLA / net cash outflow over 30 days ≥ 100%  ·  NSFR = available stable funding / required stable funding ≥ 100%
summary.commonMistake: Swapping the horizons of the two ratios. LCR is the 30-day shock; NSFR is the one-year structure.

application.title: Reading the funding mix
application.message: Look at the share of short-term wholesale funding and how concentrated the maturity profile is. Those two numbers say more about survival than the total stock of liquid assets.

sections.text: Before 2008, the question regulation cared about most was whether a bank had enough capital. After Lehman Brothers and Northern Rock, a second question became equally central: does the bank have enough cash at the moment it is needed? That is why Basel III created two ratios devoted entirely to liquidity.
LCR and NSFR: the short horizon and the long one

sections.title: Liquidity Coverage Ratio
sections.label: LCR
sections.denominator: Expected net cash outflow over a 30-day stress period

variables.name: High-Quality Liquid Assets
variables.description: Cash, central bank reserves, government bonds - fast to convert and stable in value even when markets are under stress

example.title: Reading the result
example.explanation: The bank holds enough liquid assets to absorb a stressed 30-day withdrawal scenario without having to dump illiquid assets at fire-sale prices.

sections.label: NSFR looks further out than LCR
sections.text: LCR only answers the question about the next thirty days. NSFR asks the longer one: is the bank's funding structure sustainable over a year, or is it quietly using short-term debt to feed long-dated assets - exactly the structure that brought down Northern Rock, a bank that passed every traditional capital test.
Computing LCR on a concrete balance sheet

The bank holds 1,000 of stable retail deposits and 200 of wholesale funding, against 100 of high-quality liquid assets after haircuts. The regulatory scenario assigns a run-off rate to each category: 5% on retail deposits, 40% on wholesale funding. The 30-day outflow is 1,000 × 5% + 200 × 40% = 50 + 80 = 130. The bank also expects 50 of inflows, but inflows count only up to 75% of outflows - the cap here is 97.5, so all 50 count. Net outflow is 80, and LCR = 100 / 80 = 125%.

sections.label: The 75% cap is not a technicality
sections.text: Without that cap, a bank could report a beautiful LCR by leaning on receivables falling due within the month - in other words by assuming that while it is in crisis, every one of its counterparties still pays on time. The cap forces at least 25% of the outflow to be covered by assets in hand rather than by other people's promises. That is the shape of the whole liquidity rulebook: every parameter is a behavioural assumption under stress, and the value of the ratio comes from every bank being made to use the same set of assumptions, so the numbers compare.

left.label: LCR - the 30-day question
left.text: Do the liquid assets cover the net cash outflow through one stressed month? This is the short-term survival metric, and its denominator is a scenario rather than a historical figure.

right.label: NSFR - the one-year question
right.text: Does the available stable funding cover the stable funding the asset mix requires? This is a structural metric: it asks whether the bank is financing long assets with short money to a dangerous degree, not what happens next month.

lines: Having enough capital does not mean having enough liquidity - two independent risks needing two separate sets of metrics.
Next lesson: when LCR and NSFR start flashing, the bank needs a concrete playbook - the contingency funding plan.
